task: R1 can ping server 10.0.20.10 using its transit source, but LAN clients cannot. R1 owns 10.0.10.1 on Gi0/0. Send a ping to the server using that LAN address as the source.

teaching.hint: Change the reply destination while keeping the remote target unchanged.
teaching.takeaway: A sourced ping tests the return path toward 10.0.10.1. It still originates on R1, so success does not establish that a particular client’s access path and policy work.

task: Small pings to 10.0.20.10 succeed, but large transfers stall. On IOS supporting this one-line form, send five 1500-byte IPv4 datagrams without permitting fragmentation.

teaching.hint: Control packet size and prevent routers from fragmenting this IPv4 probe.
teaching.takeaway: A fragmentation-needed response is positive size-limit evidence; a timeout could also be loss or filtering. The IOS size is the IP datagram size, unlike a host tool’s payload-size field.

task: R1 has an installed route to 10.0.20.10, but probes fail. Use the IOS command that reveals responding hops toward that numeric destination.

teaching.hint: Choose a path observation, rather than another local route-table display.
teaching.takeaway: Asterisks mean the probes received no usable reply in time. Later responding hops show why silence at one hop does not by itself prove a forwarding failure there.

task: Traffic is intermittently lost across R1 Gi0/1 even though it is up/up. Display that interface’s speed, duplex and detailed error counters before changing the route.

teaching.hint: The brief IP table cannot show whether new receive errors are accumulating.
teaching.takeaway: Compare counter increments over the same interval at both ends. An up/up link can still carry errors; one old CRC total cannot identify the current fault or prove a damaged cable.

task: Several outages coincide with reported link changes. On IOS supporting output filters, display buffered log lines containing the exact uppercase text LINK without changing logging configuration.

teaching.hint: Use a display filter; the matching text is case-sensitive.
teaching.takeaway: This view omits nonmatching messages, including separate LINEPROTO events. Correlate timestamps and inspect the unfiltered context before attributing an outage to a particular cause.

task: An IPv4 neighbor entry identifies client MAC 0001.9612.0a11. On SW1, look up that exact MAC to identify its learned VLAN and port before checking the endpoint’s attachment.

teaching.hint: Use the switch’s forwarding table, not another IP-to-MAC lookup.
teaching.takeaway: A trunk result points toward another switch, so continue the trace there. The learned entry records where source traffic was seen; it does not verify the client’s mask or gateway.

task: PC-A is 10.0.10.50. A server-side capture shows its request arrived and the reply left toward R2, yet PC-A receives nothing. On R2, inspect the installed route chosen for that exact reply destination.

teaching.hint: Look up the affected host, because a more-specific route can override its subnet route.
teaching.takeaway: The selected return prefix and next hop are the evidence you need. A working route to another client—or a router’s own sourced ping—can miss a host-specific discard route.
